questions.prompt: How many books make up the Catholic canon of Scripture in total?
questions.explanation: The Catholic canon includes 46 books of the Old Testament and 27 of the New Testament, for a total of 73 -- discerned by the Church through apostolic Tradition.
questions.hint: It's 46 Old Testament books plus 27 New Testament books.

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: The Catechism teaches that Christians read the Old Testament in the light of what event?
choices: Christ crucified and risen
The fall of Jerusalem
The Babylonian exile alone
The building of the Temple
questions.correctAnswer: Christ crucified and risen
questions.explanation: CCC 129 teaches that 'Christians therefore read the Old Testament in the light of Christ crucified and risen' -- the whole of Scripture, Old and New, is read as one unified story fulfilled in Christ.
questions.hint: This is the central event of the New Testament, read back into the whole story.

citations.quote: Christians therefore read the Old Testament in the light of Christ crucified and risen.

questions.prompt: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' opens which book of the New Testament?
choices: The Gospel of John
The Gospel of Matthew
The Book of Revelation
The Letter to the Hebrews
questions.correctAnswer: The Gospel of John
questions.explanation: John 1:1 opens the Fourth Gospel with a profound statement of Christ's eternal divinity as the Word (Logos) who was with God and was God, later 'made flesh' in the Incarnation.
questions.hint: This Gospel's opening deliberately echoes the very first words of Genesis.

citations.quote: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

questions.prompt: The Bible is best described as:
choices: A library of many books, written by different human authors over centuries, with God as their ultimate author
A single book, written by one author in one sitting
A collection of myths with no historical value
A book written entirely in the last 200 years
questions.correctAnswer: A library of many books, written by different human authors over centuries, with God as their ultimate author
questions.explanation: God inspired the human authors of Scripture, who wrote in their own words, times, and literary forms -- true human authors, and yet God himself is the Bible's ultimate author.
questions.hint: Two authors are involved at once: many human ones, and one divine one.

citations.quote: God is the author of Sacred Scripture... The divinely revealed realities... have been written down under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Bible was written by a single author, across a single generation.
questions.explanation: Scripture was composed by many human authors across roughly a thousand years, in different languages and literary forms -- yet it holds together as one unified word, since God inspired all of it.
questions.hint: Think of how many different named authors' names appear across the Bible's books.

citations.quote: God is the author of Sacred Scripture... The divinely revealed realities... have been written down under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: The Bible is divided into two main parts: the Old Testament and the ____ Testament.
questions.correctAnswer: New
questions.explanation: The Old Testament records God's covenant with Israel before Christ; the New Testament records Christ's life and the apostolic Church founded on him.
questions.hint: It's the counterpart to 'Old.'

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: What does the Catechism teach about the human authors of Scripture?
choices: God chose them and employed them as true authors, using their own faculties and powers, while he himself remains the book's principal author
They were mere secretaries with no real authorial role of their own
They wrote independently of any divine involvement
Their individual personalities and styles are absent from the text
questions.correctAnswer: God chose them and employed them as true authors, using their own faculties and powers, while he himself remains the book's principal author
questions.explanation: Inspiration does not erase the human author's mind, style, or historical situation; it works through them. This is why Paul's letters sound like Paul and the Psalms carry real human anguish and joy, even while the whole is genuinely God's own word.
questions.hint: Ask whether inspiration bypasses the human writer or works through him.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catechism teaches that God is the author of both Testaments.
questions.explanation: True, and it matters against a lingering assumption that the Old Testament is somehow a lesser or superseded text. Both Testaments have God as their author and both retain permanent value, even though the Old is read in light of the New's fulfillment of it.
questions.hint: Ask whether authorship of Scripture is divided between the Testaments or shared across both.

questions.prompt: What does 'inerrancy' mean as the Church actually teaches it?
choices: Scripture teaches, without error, the truth God wanted put into it for the sake of our salvation
Every sentence in the Bible is a precise scientific or historical claim
The Bible contains no figurative or poetic language whatsoever
Inerrancy applies only to the New Testament
questions.correctAnswer: Scripture teaches, without error, the truth God wanted put into it for the sake of our salvation
questions.explanation: Dei Verbum's own careful wording is that Scripture teaches without error the truth for the sake of salvation — a claim about the saving truth God intended, not a blanket claim that every incidental detail is a modern scientific report.
questions.hint: The Church's own document qualifies exactly what the 'without error' claim is about.

questions.prompt: Match each basic term about Scripture to what it actually claims.

pairs.right: God as principal author, working through real human authors
Scripture teaches without error the truth for our salvation
The complete, authoritative list of the Bible's books
Both authored by God, read together, neither superseding the other's authorship

questions.explanation: Each of these terms is regularly overstated or understated in casual conversation. Precision here is what lets someone answer 'doesn't the Bible have errors' without either dodging the question or conceding more than the Church actually claims.
questions.hint: One concerns authorship, one concerns truthfulness, one concerns the list of books, one concerns both Testaments together.

questions.prompt: The first five books of the Old Testament -- Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy -- are together called the:
choices: Torah (or Pentateuch)
Wisdom Literature
Minor Prophets
Historical Books
questions.correctAnswer: Torah (or Pentateuch)
questions.explanation: 'Pentateuch' comes from Greek for 'five scrolls'; 'Torah' is the Hebrew term, meaning 'instruction' or 'law' -- together these five books form the foundation of the whole Old Testament.
questions.hint: 'Penta-' is the Greek prefix for 'five.'

citations.quote: It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books. This complete list is called the canon of Scripture.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Book of Genesis contains two distinct creation accounts.
questions.explanation: Genesis opens with two complementary accounts of creation -- the six-day account in chapter 1, and a second account beginning in chapter 2 that focuses on the creation of man and woman.
questions.hint: Look closely at chapters 1 and 2 -- the story of creation is told a second time, from a different angle.

citations.quote: This is the story of the heavens and the earth at their creation. When the LORD God made the earth and the heavens

questions.prompt: God's covenant with Israel at Mount Sinai included the ____ Commandments, given to Moses.
questions.correctAnswer: Ten
questions.explanation: The Ten Commandments, given at Sinai, form the heart of the Old Covenant's moral law -- a law the Catechism treats as still binding in its substance under the New Covenant.
questions.hint: It's the same number of Commandments taught in every catechism class.

citations.quote: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me.

questions.prompt: The 'Major Prophets' of the Old Testament include Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and:
choices: Daniel
Amos
Hosea
Malachi
questions.correctAnswer: Daniel
questions.explanation: The 'Major' and 'Minor' Prophets are distinguished by the length of their books, not by their relative importance -- Amos, Hosea, and Malachi belong instead to the twelve 'Minor Prophets.'
questions.hint: 'Major' here is about book length, not spiritual importance.

citations.quote: Through the prophets, God forms his people in the hope of salvation, in the expectation of a new and everlasting Covenant intended for all, to be written on their hearts.

questions.prompt: True or False: The prophets' central message was primarily to predict specific future events centuries in advance, with little concern for calling Israel back to covenant faithfulness in their own time.
questions.explanation: The prophets primarily called Israel to repentance and covenant fidelity in their own historical moment -- messianic hope for the future is part of their message, but not its whole focus.
questions.hint: Prophets were, first of all, preachers to their own generation, not just fortune-tellers for the future.

citations.quote: Jesus' call to conversion and penance, like that of the prophets before him, does not aim first at outward works... but at the conversion of the heart, interior conversion.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The first five books of the Bible
Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel
A sacred bond God establishes with his people
Israel's deliverance from slavery in Egypt

questions.explanation: These four terms cover the backbone of Old Testament history -- its founding books, its major prophetic voices, its central theological concept, and its defining act of deliverance.
questions.hint: One is a group of books, one a group of prophets, one a theological concept, one a historical event.

citations.quote: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; you shall have no other gods before me.

questions.prompt: What is the literary genre of most of the Book of Psalms?
choices: Poetry — prayers and hymns meant to be sung or recited, using Hebrew parallelism rather than rhyme
Legal code
Historical narrative with precise chronology
Prophetic oracle addressed to foreign nations
questions.correctAnswer: Poetry — prayers and hymns meant to be sung or recited, using Hebrew parallelism rather than rhyme
questions.explanation: Hebrew poetry works by parallelism — restating, contrasting, or building on an idea in a second line — rather than by rhyme, which is why the Psalms translate into other languages more successfully than most poetry does: the structure survives translation.
questions.hint: Ask what structural device Hebrew poetry relies on instead of rhyme.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Wisdom literature (Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes, and others) is primarily concerned with predicting future historical events.
questions.explanation: False. Wisdom literature reflects on how to live well, on suffering, and on the meaning of life — practical and reflective, not predictive. Confusing it with prophetic literature misreads its entire purpose.
questions.hint: Ask whether these books are oriented toward the future or toward how to live now.

questions.prompt: The Book of Job wrestles above all with the question of innocent ____, without offering a single tidy resolution to the problem.
questions.correctAnswer: suffering
questions.explanation: Job is notable precisely for what it does not do: it never gives Job (or the reader) a clean explanation for his suffering. God's answer from the whirlwind reframes the question rather than answering it directly, which is part of why the book still speaks so powerfully to real grief.
questions.hint: The whole book centers on why a righteous man endures terrible loss.

questions.prompt: Match each Old Testament category to its characteristic content.

pairs.right: Law and founding narrative, Genesis through Deuteronomy
Israel's story from the conquest through the exile and return
Reflection on how to live, and on suffering and meaning
God's word calling Israel to fidelity, not primarily prediction

questions.explanation: Note the last two categories are both frequently misread the same way — as though their purpose were forecasting the future — when both are actually oriented toward present fidelity and present meaning.
questions.hint: Two of these four categories are commonly mistaken for being about predicting the future.

questions.prompt: The first three Gospels -- Matthew, Mark, and Luke -- are called the 'Synoptic Gospels' because they:
choices: Share a similar structure, content, and viewpoint, and so can be 'seen together'
Were all written by the same single author
Are the only Gospels considered inspired
Were written after the Gospel of John
questions.correctAnswer: Share a similar structure, content, and viewpoint, and so can be 'seen together'
questions.explanation: 'Synoptic' comes from Greek meaning 'seen together' -- these three Gospels share substantial overlapping material and can be usefully compared side by side, unlike John's distinct approach.
questions.hint: 'Syn-optic' literally means 'together-view.'

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Gospel of John is typically grouped together with Matthew, Mark, and Luke as one of the 'Synoptic Gospels.'
questions.explanation: John stands apart from the other three, with a distinct structure, style, and theological emphasis -- it is not counted among the Synoptics.
questions.hint: This is the one Gospel that stands apart from the other three, stylistically.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: The Catechism describes the Gospels as the 'heart of all the Scriptures' because they are our principal source for the life and ____ of the Incarnate Word.
questions.correctAnswer: teaching
questions.explanation: Everything else in Scripture -- Old and New Testament alike -- is read in relation to the Gospels, since they record Christ's own words and deeds most directly.
questions.hint: Alongside 'life,' this word is what the Gospels record about Christ's own words.

citations.quote: The Gospels are the heart of all the Scriptures 'because they are our principal source for the life and teaching of the Incarnate Word, our Saviour.'

questions.prompt: The Catechism describes the formation of the Gospels happening in three stages: the life and teaching of Jesus, the oral Tradition of the apostles, and finally:
choices: The Gospels being written down by the four evangelists
The Gospels being translated into Latin
The Council of Trent formally approving them
The invention of the printing press
questions.correctAnswer: The Gospels being written down by the four evangelists
questions.explanation: The evangelists, drawing on the earlier oral preaching of the apostolic Church, put this apostolic testimony into writing, 'selecting' and 'synthesizing' it for their particular communities.
questions.hint: This is the final stage, after Jesus' own ministry and the apostles' preaching about it.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Church requires every one of the four evangelists to have personally witnessed the entirety of Jesus' earthly ministry firsthand.
questions.explanation: The Gospels' reliability rests on their rootedness in apostolic testimony passed down faithfully, not on a requirement that every individual evangelist personally witnessed every event they recorded.
questions.hint: What matters is the Gospels' connection to apostolic testimony as a whole, not each author's personal presence at every event.

citations.quote: the four Gospels... faithfully hand on what Jesus, the Son of God, while he lived among men, really did and taught for their eternal salvation.

questions.prompt: Match each Gospel to a distinguishing note about it.

pairs.right: Written with a strongly Jewish audience and Old Testament fulfillment in mind
Shortest Gospel, fast-paced, emphasizing Christ's suffering servanthood
Emphasizes mercy, the poor, and salvation's universal reach
Distinct in style, emphasizing Christ's divinity and 'I am' statements

questions.explanation: Each evangelist writes with his own emphasis and audience in mind, while all four together present one coherent portrait of Christ.
questions.hint: One is Jewish-focused, one is fast and Passion-focused, one favors the poor, one is theologically distinct.

citations.quote: The Gospels are the heart of all the Scriptures 'because they are our principal source for the life and teaching of the Incarnate Word, our Saviour.'

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the Gospel of John most sharply from the Synoptic Gospels in its portrait of Jesus?
choices: John emphasizes lengthy discourses and explicit statements of Jesus's divine identity ('I am' sayings), where the Synoptics favor parables and shorter sayings
John omits the crucifixion entirely
John is the only Gospel written by a non-eyewitness
John contains no miracles, unlike the Synoptics
questions.correctAnswer: John emphasizes lengthy discourses and explicit statements of Jesus's divine identity ('I am' sayings), where the Synoptics favor parables and shorter sayings
questions.explanation: John's high Christology is stated openly and often (I am the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd), where the Synoptics let Jesus's identity emerge more gradually through action and parable — a real difference in approach, not a contradiction between them.
questions.hint: Compare how directly each Gospel has Jesus state who he is.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catechism describes the Gospels as arising in three identifiable stages: the life and teaching of Jesus, the apostolic preaching, and the written composition by the evangelists.
questions.explanation: True, and this three-stage account is the Church's own careful answer to how eyewitness memory, oral proclamation, and finally written text relate to each other — it neither treats the Gospels as raw transcripts nor as late inventions disconnected from the events.
questions.hint: The three stages move from an event, through preaching, to a written text.

questions.prompt: The Catechism calls the Gospels the '____ of all the Scriptures,' because they are our principal source for Christ's life and teaching.
questions.correctAnswer: heart
questions.explanation: Calling the Gospels the heart of Scripture does not diminish the rest of the Bible; it names their central place, since everything else in Scripture is read in relation to the Christ the Gospels present directly.
questions.hint: The metaphor names the Gospels' central place among all of Scripture's books.

questions.prompt: Match each Gospel to a distinguishing note about it.

pairs.right: Written with a strong eye to Jesus fulfilling Old Testament prophecy
The shortest Gospel, likely the earliest written
Paired with Acts, with particular attention to the marginalized
High Christology, extended discourses, and 'I am' sayings

questions.explanation: Each evangelist writes with a real theological emphasis and a particular audience in mind, without contradicting the others — four true, complementary portraits of one Christ, not four competing or inconsistent accounts.
questions.hint: Each has one especially recognizable feature: brevity, fulfillment, companionship with a second book, or explicit theology.

questions.prompt: The largest single block of New Testament letters was written by:
choices: St. Paul
St. Peter
St. John
St. James
questions.correctAnswer: St. Paul
questions.explanation: Paul's letters to various churches and individuals -- Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, and many more -- make up the largest portion of the New Testament's epistolary literature.
questions.hint: This apostle's missionary journeys generated letters to many of the churches he founded.

citations.quote: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God

questions.prompt: True or False: The Letter to the Romans is widely regarded as containing Paul's most systematic presentation of the Gospel and the doctrine of justification.
questions.explanation: Romans opens with Paul's programmatic statement that he is 'not ashamed of the gospel,' since 'the righteous shall live by faith' -- launching one of Scripture's most sustained theological arguments.
questions.hint: This letter is often called Paul's theological masterwork.

citations.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel. It is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes... For in it is revealed the righteousness of God from faith to faith; as it is written, 'The one who is righteous by faith will live.'

questions.prompt: The Letter to the Hebrews presents Christ as the perfect and eternal ____ Priest, superior to the Levitical priesthood of the Old Covenant.
questions.correctAnswer: High
questions.explanation: Hebrews argues at length that Christ's priesthood, offered once for all, fulfills and surpasses the repeated sacrifices of the Old Covenant's priesthood.
questions.hint: This title pairs with 'priest' to describe the very highest priestly office.

citations.quote: We have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God... one who has similarly been tested in every way, yet without sin.

questions.prompt: The 'Catholic Epistles' (James, 1-2 Peter, 1-3 John, Jude) are called 'Catholic' meaning:
choices: Universal or general, addressed broadly rather than to one specific local church
Written exclusively by popes
Approved only at the Council of Trent
Written in Latin rather than Greek
questions.correctAnswer: Universal or general, addressed broadly rather than to one specific local church
questions.explanation: Unlike Paul's letters, which typically address a specific community (Rome, Corinth, Galatia), these letters are addressed more broadly -- hence 'catholic,' meaning 'universal.'
questions.hint: 'Catholic' here carries its original Greek meaning -- 'according to the whole,' or universal.

citations.quote: James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the dispersion, greetings.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Letter of James teaches that faith without works is dead.
questions.explanation: James 2:17 states plainly: 'faith of itself, if it does not have works, is dead.' The letter insists genuine faith must show itself alive through concrete action.
questions.hint: This is one of the most direct statements in the New Testament connecting faith and action.

citations.quote: So also faith of itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

questions.prompt: Match each letter to its key theme.

pairs.right: Justification by grace through faith, systematically explained
Christ as the eternal High Priest
Faith must be shown alive through works
God is love, and love of neighbor flows from love of God

questions.explanation: Each New Testament letter addresses its own pressing pastoral concern, together forming a rich theological witness alongside the Gospels.
questions.hint: One is about justification, one about priesthood, one about works, one about love.

citations.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel. It is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes... For in it is revealed the righteousness of God from faith to faith; as it is written, 'The one who is righteous by faith will live.'
So also faith of itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

questions.prompt: What is the central theme of Paul's Letter to the Galatians?
choices: Justification comes through faith in Christ, not through works of the Mosaic Law such as circumcision
The order of offices in the local church
The proper conduct of the Eucharistic assembly
A detailed philosophical argument for God's existence
questions.correctAnswer: Justification comes through faith in Christ, not through works of the Mosaic Law such as circumcision
questions.explanation: Galatians is Paul at his most polemical, responding to a specific crisis: some were insisting Gentile converts be circumcised and keep the Mosaic Law. Paul's forceful response shaped how the Church has read the relationship of faith, grace, and the Law ever since.
questions.hint: This letter responds to a specific controversy about circumcision and the Mosaic Law.

questions.prompt: True or False: Revelation (the Apocalypse) is written primarily to satisfy curiosity about the precise timeline of future events.
questions.explanation: False. Revelation is apocalyptic literature written to encourage a persecuted Church with the assurance that God's sovereignty will triumph — its symbolic imagery is meant to console and exhort suffering Christians, not to function as a coded almanac of future dates.
questions.hint: Ask what a persecuted first-century audience most needed to hear from this book.

questions.prompt: The Letter to the Hebrews presents Christ as the perfect and eternal High ____, superior to the Levitical priesthood he fulfills.
questions.correctAnswer: Priest
questions.explanation: Hebrews' whole argument builds toward this: the old priesthood offered repeated sacrifices that could never fully take away sin, where Christ's single, perfect self-offering accomplishes once for all what the Levitical system could only foreshadow.
questions.hint: The letter compares Christ's role to the Old Testament priesthood, and finds him superior to it.

questions.prompt: Match each New Testament letter to its central theme.

pairs.right: Justification by faith, not by works of the Law
Christ as the perfect and eternal High Priest
Faith without works is dead
Assurance of God's sovereignty for a persecuted Church

questions.explanation: Read together, Galatians and James have sometimes been read as though they contradict each other on faith and works — they do not, once each is read for the specific error it is actually correcting rather than pitted against the other in the abstract.
questions.hint: Two of these letters are sometimes wrongly read as contradicting each other on faith and works.

questions.prompt: The Catechism lists several senses of Scripture beyond the literal sense. Together these additional senses are called the:
choices: Spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, and anagogical)
Historical senses
Apocryphal senses
Vernacular senses
questions.correctAnswer: Spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, and anagogical)
questions.explanation: Beyond the literal sense (what the words directly mean), Catholic tradition reads Scripture for its spiritual senses -- how it points to Christ, teaches right action, and points toward our final destiny.
questions.hint: Three senses, all beyond the plain literal meaning of the words.

citations.quote: According to an ancient tradition, one can distinguish between two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, the latter being subdivided into the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

questions.prompt: True or False: The 'literal sense' of Scripture, in Catholic interpretation, means always reading every passage as a strict, scientifically precise historical report, regardless of its literary form.
questions.explanation: The literal sense means the meaning conveyed by the words themselves, discovered through sound interpretation that respects the author's own literary form -- poetry, parable, and historical narrative are all read according to what they actually are.
questions.hint: The literal sense respects what kind of writing a passage actually is -- poem, parable, history, and so on.

citations.quote: The literal sense is the meaning conveyed by the words of Scripture and discovered by exegesis, following the rules of sound interpretation.

questions.prompt: The Catechism teaches that Sacred Scripture must be read and interpreted 'in the light of the same ____' by which it was written -- that is, with the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
questions.correctAnswer: Spirit
questions.explanation: Because the Holy Spirit inspired Scripture's human authors, faithful interpretation requires reading it in that same Spirit, within the living Tradition of the Church that first received it.
questions.hint: This is the same divine Person who inspired the biblical authors in the first place.

citations.quote: Sacred Scripture must be read and interpreted in the light of the same Spirit by whom it was written.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the Catechism's three criteria for interpreting Scripture 'in accordance with the Spirit'?
choices: Purely private interpretation, independent of the Church's living Tradition
Attention to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture
Reading Scripture within the living Tradition of the Church
Attention to the analogy of faith
questions.correctAnswer: Purely private interpretation, independent of the Church's living Tradition
questions.explanation: The Catechism's three actual criteria all situate the individual reader within the Church's living Tradition and the coherence of the whole faith -- not apart from it.
questions.hint: Three of these four criteria all point back to the Church's own living Tradition; one explicitly cuts against it.

citations.quote: Be especially attentive 'to the content and unity of the whole Scripture'... read the Scripture within 'the living Tradition of the whole Church'... be attentive to the analogy of faith.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catechism teaches that all the books and parts of Scripture are one, because all of Scripture is inspired by one and the same God.
questions.explanation: This is the first of the Catechism's criteria for interpreting Scripture -- reading with attention to the content and unity of the whole, since one divine author stands behind every book.
questions.hint: This is about Scripture's underlying unity, despite its many human authors and books.

citations.quote: Be especially attentive 'to the content and unity of the whole Scripture,' [since] Scripture is a unity by reason of the unity of God's plan, of which Christ Jesus is the center and heart.

questions.prompt: Match each sense of Scripture to its focus.

pairs.right: The meaning intended by the human author's own words
How events and figures point to Christ
How Scripture teaches us to act justly
How realities point toward our eternal destiny

questions.explanation: These four senses, working together, let the same passage of Scripture speak on multiple levels at once -- what it plainly says, and what it points beyond itself toward.
questions.hint: One sense is about the plain words; three others point toward Christ, right action, or eternity.

citations.quote: According to an ancient tradition, one can distinguish between two senses of Scripture: the literal and the spiritual, the latter being subdivided into the allegorical, moral and anagogical senses.

questions.prompt: Why does the Catechism insist that attention to the literal sense must come before any spiritual reading?
choices: Because the spiritual senses build on and presuppose what the human author actually intended to convey, rather than replacing it
Because the spiritual senses are unnecessary once the literal sense is established
Because the literal sense is the only sense the Church actually endorses
Because the spiritual senses were invented independently of the literal text
questions.correctAnswer: Because the spiritual senses build on and presuppose what the human author actually intended to convey, rather than replacing it
questions.explanation: A spiritual reading detached from the literal sense becomes arbitrary — anything could mean anything. Grounding the spiritual senses in the literal sense first is what keeps typology and allegory disciplined rather than free-floating.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to spiritual interpretation if it had no anchor in what the text actually says.

questions.prompt: True or False: The 'moral sense' of Scripture concerns what a passage teaches us to do, for a just life.
questions.explanation: True. Alongside the allegorical sense (Christ's presence in the text) and the anagogical sense (its meaning for our eternal destiny), the moral sense asks what a passage teaches about acting justly here and now — a practical dimension of reading Scripture.
questions.hint: Of the three spiritual senses, this one concerns present action.

questions.prompt: What are the Catechism's three criteria for interpreting Scripture 'in accordance with the Spirit who inspired it'?
choices: Attention to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture, reading within the living Tradition of the Church, and being attentive to the analogy of faith
Attention only to the original Hebrew or Greek grammar
Consulting only the earliest surviving manuscripts
Relying exclusively on a single Church Father's interpretation
questions.correctAnswer: Attention to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture, reading within the living Tradition of the Church, and being attentive to the analogy of faith
questions.explanation: These three criteria work together to prevent an isolated verse from being read against the coherence of the whole: unity keeps a passage from contradicting the rest of the Bible, Tradition keeps interpretation from floating free of the Church's living understanding, and the analogy of faith checks a reading against the connection of all doctrines to each other.
questions.hint: One criterion concerns the whole Bible, one concerns the Church's living understanding, one concerns doctrine's own coherence.

questions.prompt: Match each sense of Scripture to its focus.

pairs.right: What the human author intended to convey
How the events point to Christ
How the text teaches us to act justly
How the text points to our eternal destiny

questions.explanation: The three spiritual senses do not compete with the literal sense; they build on it. A reading that skips the literal sense entirely, moving straight to allegory, has lost the anchor the Catechism insists on keeping.
questions.hint: Three of these are the 'spiritual senses,' built on the foundation of the first.

questions.prompt: Trent's Fourth Session (1546) formally closed the Old Testament canon, affirming books the Reformers rejected as a shorter, 'protocanonical-only' list. What does 'deuterocanonical' mean, applied to books like Tobit, Judith, and Wisdom?
choices: Books whose canonicity was affirmed later and more explicitly than the protocanonical books, not books added or invented at Trent
Books that were written after the New Testament closed
Books accepted by Protestants but rejected by Catholics
Books that were never used in the Church before 1546
questions.correctAnswer: Books whose canonicity was affirmed later and more explicitly than the protocanonical books, not books added or invented at Trent

questions.prompt: Scholars use critical editions like Nestle-Aland's Novum Testamentum Graece and the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia, while the Roman liturgy uses the Church's own Nova Vulgata (1979) as its official reference text. Why can the Church use a different 'typical edition' for worship without contradicting the scholarship?
choices: A liturgical typical edition serves the Church's need for a single, stable, authoritative text for public worship, while critical editions serve ongoing textual-critical scholarship -- different purposes, not competing claims about which is 'true'
The Nova Vulgata rejects the findings of modern textual criticism entirely
Critical editions and the Nova Vulgata are identical documents under different names

questions.correctAnswer: A liturgical typical edition serves the Church's need for a single, stable, authoritative text for public worship, while critical editions serve ongoing textual-critical scholarship -- different purposes, not competing claims about which is 'true'
questions.explanation: The Nova Vulgata, promulgated in 1979, actually draws on modern critical scholarship in its preparation while serving a specifically liturgical function: providing one stable, authoritative text for the Roman Rite's public worship. Critical editions like NA28 and BHS serve the different, ongoing purpose of tracking and weighing manuscript evidence -- the two coexist because they answer different needs, not because one refutes the other.
questions.hint: Ask what job each edition is actually doing, rather than assuming only one can be 'the real Bible.'
